reason: The cited evidence (E1-E3) concerns corrosion of laser-clad or laser-melted high-entropy alloy coatings on Q235, not the effect of surface defect density on the native Q235 steel itself. None of the passages provide specific prior evidence that surface defects on Q235 act as preferential anodic sites, that defect density controls passive film breakdown on Q235, or that laser patterning can isolate defect density as a variable on this steel. The key premises are therefore unsupported by the cited literature.
premises: Surface defects act as preferential anodic sites on Q235 steel
Higher defect density promotes early breakdown of the passive oxide film
Laser patterning can controllably increase surface defect density without significant unintended changes
Defect-driven passive film breakdown accelerates localized corrosion in chloride environments
EIS polarization resistance and SKP potential maps can detect these defect-driven corrosion differences
